1.1 Language Overview and Execution Model
flash.back: Covers what Python is, how it actually runs, the feature and limitation lists from the notes, and the two foundational claims the notes open with: Python is dynamically typed, and in Python everything is an object.

flash.front: 1.1.1 What Python Is
flash.back: General purpose — Python is not tied to one problem domain. The same language is used for scripting, web backends, automation, data analysis, machine learning, testing, GUIs and glue code. Contrast with domain-specific languages: SQL only queries data, HTML only describes documents, MATLAB targets numerical work.

flash.front: 1.1.2 Dynamically Typed Language
flash.back: You never declare a type. You bind a name to a value, and the type belongs to the value (the object), not to the name. The name is only a label pointing at an object; rebinding it to a different kind of object is legal.

flash.front: 1.1.3 In Python, Everything Is an Object
flash.back: Every value you can bind to a name is an object, and every object has three things: an identity (its address, via id()), a type, and a value. Crucially this includes things that are not objects in most other languages: functions, methods, classes, modules, and even types themselves.

flash.front: 1.1.4 Interpreted — the Execution Model
flash.back: The note lists interpreted as a feature. What actually happens is a two-stage process, and knowing both stages explains several behaviours later in the notebook.

flash.front: 1.1.5 Features of Python
flash.back:
The interpreter absorbs the OS differences — path separators, line endings, system calls —
so your source does not have to.

flash.front: 1.1.6 Limitations of Python
flash.back: Going deeper — CPython also offers an optional free-threaded build that removes the GIL entirely, distinct from the standard build most people actually run. "The GIL always applies" describes that standard build specifically, not an absolute rule for every CPython build. See 17.5 for the timed proof of the GIL's CPU-bound-vs-I/O-bound effect, and for how that proof changes on the free-threaded build.

flash.front: 1.3 Syntax, Statements and Code Structure
flash.back: Statements — A statement is a complete instruction Python executes (an assignment, a function call, a return, an import, etc.). Normally one statement per line; ; lets you chain multiple statements on one line (discouraged), and a line ending in \, or an unclosed bracket, lets a single statement continue across multiple lines.

flash.front: 1.4 Basic Input and Output
flash.back: Output — print() — Prints any number of values to standard output, converting each to its string form automatically. sep (default " ") controls the separator between values; end (default "\n") controls what is written after the last one.

flash.front: 2.1 Overview of Built-in Data Types
flash.back: Object — every value in Python is an object. Every object has an identity (id()), a type (type()) and a value; each data type below is simply a built-in category of object, with its own value representation and behaviour.

flash.front: 2.2 Basic Data Types
flash.back: These are the 5 basic data types in Python — int, float, bool, str and complex. All five are immutable: once created, the object itself can never be changed — a name bound to one always points to that single object, and anything that looks like a modification actually creates a new object and rebinds the name to it.

flash.front: 2.2.1 Integers (int)
flash.back: Python has three numeric types — int, float and complex (defined in 2.1). Of the three, int is the only one with multiple literal forms, since a whole number can be written in decimal, binary, octal or hexadecimal and still be the exact same value/object.

flash.front: 2.2.2 Floating-Point Numbers (float)
flash.back: Why — float is stored as binary floating-point (IEEE 754), and most decimal fractions (including 0.1 and 0.2) have no exact binary representation, the same way 1/3 has no exact finite decimal representation. Each is stored as the closest representable binary value, so arithmetic on them accumulates tiny rounding error. Never compare floats with ==; use math.isclose() instead.

flash.front: 2.2.3 Booleans (bool)
flash.back: Common mistake — treating bool as an unrelated type. In fact bool is a subclass of int — True/False behave as 1/0 in arithmetic, and isinstance(True, int) is True.

flash.front: 2.3 Composite Data Types
flash.back: These are the 8 composite data types in Python — list, tuple, set, frozenset, dict, bytes, bytearray and range. Unlike the basic types (2.2), mutability varies by type: list, set, dict and bytearray are mutable; tuple, frozenset, bytes and range are immutable.

flash.front: 2.3.1 Lists (list)
flash.back: An ordered, mutable collection of items. Day-to-day operations — indexing, slicing, methods, comprehensions — are covered in depth in 5.1.

flash.front: 2.3.2 Tuples (tuple)
flash.back: An ordered, immutable collection of items. Day-to-day operations — unpacking, methods, hashability — are covered in depth in 5.5.

flash.front: 2.3.3 Sets (set)
flash.back: An unordered, mutable collection of unique items. Day-to-day operations — methods, mathematical set operations, hashing — are covered in depth in 5.3.

flash.front: 2.3.4 Frozensets (frozenset)
flash.back: An unordered, immutable collection of unique items. Covered alongside set in 5.3, including why immutability makes it hashable.

flash.front: 2.3.5 Dictionaries (dict)
flash.back: A collection of key-value pairs, insertion-ordered. Day-to-day operations — methods, comprehension, hashing — are covered in depth in 5.4.

flash.back: Each element is a single byte — an integer in the range 0 to 255 (a byte is 8 bits, i.e. 2⁸ = 256 possible values). Assigning a value outside this range raises ValueError:

flash.front: 2.4 Object Reuse and Caching (Interning)
flash.back: How reassignment works — reassigning a name does not change the existing object; it creates a new object and rebinds the name to it. If nothing else refers to the old object, it becomes eligible for garbage collection.

flash.front: 2.5 The del Statement
flash.back: del removes a name binding (or an item from a mutable container) — it does not necessarily destroy the underlying object. An object is only garbage-collected once its reference count drops to zero (2.4), so del just removes one reference; if another name still points to the same object, that object lives on.

flash.front: 3.1.6 Assignment Operators
flash.back: = also supports chained assignment (a = b = c = 5) and multiple assignment/unpacking (a, b = 1, 2).

flash.front: 3.1.7 Ternary Operators
flash.back: A conditional expression — not a statement — that picks one of two values inline: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. Because it's an expression (it evaluates to a value), it can be used anywhere a value is expected — assignment, a function argument, inside an f-string — a full if/else statement cannot. Python has no separate ?: symbol like C/Java/JavaScript; it spells the same idea out with keywords instead.

flash.front: 3.1.8 Special Operators — Identity and Membership
flash.back: Identity (is, is not) compares object identity — whether two names point to the exact same object in memory (id()) — not whether their values are equal. Two equal-value objects are usually not the same object (2.4 covers when CPython does, or doesn't, reuse an existing object).

flash.front: 4.1 Conditional Statements
flash.back: Python's conditional keywords are if, elif (optional, repeatable) and else (optional). Python has no switch/case — elif chains fill that role. At most one branch in the whole chain runs — the first one whose condition is truthy.

flash.front: 4.2.1 For Loops
flash.back: for iterates over the items of an iterable directly — no manual index/counter needed. range() (2.1) is commonly paired with it to loop a fixed number of times.

flash.front: 4.2.2 While Loops
flash.back: while repeats as long as its condition stays truthy. The loop body must eventually make the condition falsy — commonly by updating a variable the condition depends on — or the loop never stops.

flash.front: 4.3 Loop Control Statements
flash.back: pass is also used to stub out an empty function/class body while keeping it syntactically valid (6, 10 cover those).

flash.front: 4.4 The else Clause on Loops and try
flash.back: else isn't exclusive to if — for, while and try all accept an optional else block too. In every case it means the same thing: "this block ran to completion without an early exit."

flash.front: 4.5 Structural Pattern Matching (match/case)
flash.back: match/case is Python's answer to a switch statement, but considerably more powerful: instead of only comparing a value against literals, a case can check the shape of a value (unpack a sequence, pull specific fields out of a mapping or an object) in the same step as deciding whether it matches at all.

flash.front: 5.1.1 Indexing and Slicing

flash.front: 11.1 Association
flash.back: Association is the most general relationship between two objects: one object uses or interacts with another, but neither owns the other — both exist independently, before, during, and after the interaction. It's the "uses-a" relationship, as opposed to inheritance's "is-a" (chapter 12).

flash.front: 11.2 Aggregation
flash.back: Aggregation is a whole-part "has-a" relationship where the part can exist entirely independently of the whole — it's usually created outside the whole and simply handed in, the whole doesn't manage its lifecycle, and the same part can even belong to more than one whole. This is why it's called a weak association: destroying the whole leaves the part completely unaffected.

flash.front: 11.3 Composition
flash.back: Composition is a whole-part "owns-a" relationship where the part's lifecycle is tied to the whole — the whole builds its own part internally, nothing else ever holds a reference to it, and it can't outlive (or be shared outside of) the whole that made it. This is why it's called a strong association.

flash.front: 11.4 Delegation and Reuse Without Inheritance
flash.back: Delegation is when an object, instead of implementing a behavior itself, holds a reference to another object (usually via composition or aggregation) and forwards the call to it. It's a way to reuse another class's behavior through a "has-a" relationship, instead of inheritance's "is-a" (chapter 12) — the object doing the delegating isn't a kind of the thing it delegates to, it just uses one:

flash.front: 17.1 Concurrency Concepts and Terminology
flash.back: A thread, in programming, is the smallest independently-schedulable unit of execution within a running program — a single sequence of instructions the CPU works through, with its own call stack and instruction pointer. Every running program starts with exactly one thread automatically (the main thread); more can be created to run additional sequences of instructions inside the same program.

flash.front: 17.2 Multithreading
flash.back: The threading module offers three ways to get code running on another thread — picking one over another is mostly a matter of how much structure the job needs:

flash.front: 17.3 Daemon Threads
flash.back: A daemon thread is a background thread that doesn't keep the program alive — when every non-daemon thread has finished, Python exits immediately, killing any daemon threads still running, without waiting for them. A regular ("non-daemon") thread does the opposite: the program won't exit until it finishes, however long that takes.

flash.front: 17.4 Multiprocessing
flash.back: The multiprocessing module mirrors threading's API almost exactly — Process(target=fn, args=...), .start(), .join() — but each Process is a genuinely separate operating-system process, with its own private memory and its own Python interpreter, rather than another thread inside the same one. That's what buys real parallelism (17.5): two Processes can run Python bytecode on two different CPU cores at the literal same instant, which two Threads in the same process cannot.

flash.front: 17.5 The GIL and Performance Implications
flash.back: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a single lock inside CPython (the reference interpreter this material targets) that only lets one thread execute Python bytecode at a time — even on a machine with many CPU cores. This is exactly the limitation 1.1.6 mentions: multiple threads in CPython can never run Python bytecode in parallel, no matter how many cores are available.

flash.front: 17.6 Asynchronous Programming
flash.back: In practice — high-throughput web services. This single-thread, many-coroutines model is the standard architecture behind modern async Python web frameworks: FastAPI and aiohttp use asyncio under the hood to hold thousands of concurrent client connections open at once — an API gateway, a chat backend, or a webhook/notification dispatcher — without needing a dedicated OS thread per connection, which stops scaling long before that.

flash.front: 17.7 Choosing a Concurrency Model
flash.back: None of these is "the" right answer — a program can mix them (e.g. asyncio for thousands of open network connections, handing CPU-heavy parsing off to a multiprocessing pool).

flash.back: Since everything in Python is an object (1.1.3), a variable is never a box holding a value — it's a name bound to an object living elsewhere. Assignment (2.4) just attaches another name to the same object; it never copies it. An object's lifetime runs from creation until the moment nothing references it anymore, at which point Python reclaims its memory — the mechanics of exactly how are 19.2/19.3:

flash.front: 19.2 Reference Counting
flash.back: CPython's primary reclamation mechanism is simple: every object carries a hidden reference count — how many references currently point to it. The count goes up on assignment, passing as an argument, or storing in a container; it goes down when a name is reassigned, goes out of scope, or is deleted (19.4). The instant it hits zero, the object is freed immediately — no waiting, no background pass. sys.getrefcount() exposes the count directly:

flash.front: 19.3 Garbage Collection
flash.back: Reference counting alone has one blind spot: a reference cycle — two or more objects that reference each other — can leave every object in the cycle with a non-zero count forever, even after nothing outside the cycle points to any of them. Plain refcounting would leak this memory. The gc module's cyclic collector exists specifically to find and break cycles like this, running periodically alongside refcounting rather than replacing it:

flash.front: 20.1 Why Data Validation and Parsing Matter
flash.back: Data validation is checking that a piece of data actually has the shape a program expects (right types, required fields present, values within sensible ranges) before using it. Parsing is the related job of turning untyped input — JSON from an API request, a row from a config file, raw text from an LLM — into real, typed Python objects. Both matter for the same reason: any data arriving from outside the program (a user, a network call, a file) cannot be trusted to already match what the code assumes.
